summary: Describes XDR, a standard for describing and encoding data so it can move between different computer architectures. It uses implicit typing, unlike ASN.1-style explicit typing, and roughly fits the ISO presentation layer. It was distributed for information and does not establish an Internet standard.

plainLanguage.summary: XDR provides a common way to describe and encode data for exchange between different computer architectures. Its data description tells both sides what fields to expect, while its encoding specifies how those fields are represented as bytes.

subtitle: A language for describing data and a shared binary representation for exchanging it.

tldr.problem: Different computer architectures may represent data differently. Programs that exchange information need an agreed description of data and an encoding that both sides can interpret.
tldr.mechanism: XDR defines a C-like language for describing data types and a binary encoding that uses four-byte units, big-endian integers, and zero padding for values that do not fill a unit.
tldr.outcome: The RFC describes a standard that Sun Microsystems and others were using and proposes it for consideration by the Internet community. It does not itself establish an Internet standard.

today: RFC 1014 describes a standard that Sun Microsystems and others were using and proposed for Internet community consideration. The unit metadata records its status as Unknown and lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: What XDR Does
sections.content:
External Data Representation (XDR) is a language for describing data formats and a standard encoding for that data. The RFC says it has been used to exchange data between different computer architectures, and that Sun RPC and NFS use it to describe their data.

XDR describes data but is not a programming language. Its types are implicit in the agreed description: the encoded data does not carry a separate type field for each value. The RFC assumes that eight-bit bytes can be transferred between machines without changing their meaning.
sections.plainLanguage: XDR lets two programs agree on the structure and byte representation of data they exchange. They use the description to interpret the encoded values.

sections.title: Four-Byte Units and Padding
sections.content:
XDR represents each item using a multiple of four bytes. If a value uses a number of bytes that is not a multiple of four, zero bytes are added to fill the final unit. Bytes are read or written in sequence, with each byte preceding the next.

The RFC explains that XDR uses one byte order, big-endian, so a separate protocol does not have to identify the byte order. It chose four-byte units as a compromise between small encodings and alignment needs. Zero padding ensures that the same data has the same encoded form on different machines.
sections.plainLanguage: XDR stores data in units that are multiples of four bytes. It fills unused space with zeros so the same data has a consistent encoding.

sections.title: XDR Data Types
sections.content:
The language describes integers, enumerations, booleans, floating-point numbers, opaque byte sequences, strings, arrays, structures, unions, and optional data. A structure stores its components in declaration order. A discriminated union stores a selector value followed by the component chosen by that value.

Variable-length strings and opaque data carry a length before their bytes and are padded to a multiple of four bytes. XDR does not include representations for bit fields, bitmaps, or packed decimals. A declared maximum length is enforced when one is specified.
sections.plainLanguage: XDR provides building blocks for numbers, text, byte sequences, lists, and grouped values. The declaration order and type definitions tell the receiver how to read them.

sections.title: The XDR Description Language
sections.content:
The RFC defines XDR syntax using an extended Backus-Naur Form grammar. The language includes declarations for data types, arrays, structures, unions, constants, and type aliases. Comments use /* and */, and identifier case matters.

The RFC favors a language over diagrams because the grammar is more formal and less ambiguous, and its types correspond closely to types in languages such as C and Pascal. It includes a worked file description and shows the resulting encoded fields, including the length of a filename and zero fill bytes.
sections.plainLanguage: The grammar gives a precise way to write data layouts. Both sides can use the same declarations to understand the order and type of values in an encoded message.

items.title: Four-byte units
items.text: Items occupy a multiple of four bytes.

items.title: Zero fill
items.text: Unused space in the final unit is filled with zero bytes.

items.title: Implicit types
items.text: The data format is described separately from the encoded values.
